Chapter 6 Weak form, the Ritz and Galerkin method (šibka oblika, Ritzova in Galerkinova metoda)

6.1 Strong and weak form (močna in šibka oblika)

In chapter 4 we wrote the equilibrium of a bar in two ways. The first is an equation at every point of the bar, \(N' + q = 0\) (lemma 4.75). The second is an equality of integrals for every virtual displacement (theorem 4.76). Which of the two asks less of the unknown displacement? And what do we gain by asking less? We need the answer before we look for approximations: an approximate field is usually less smooth than the true one, and if the equation at every point does not admit it, we must write the problem differently. First we describe both forms for a bar and compare them on a bar with a step, then we do the same for a beam and for a body.

6.1.1 Boundary value problem of a bar (robni problem palice)

Take the bar from section 4.4.4 and let us collect its model in one place (figure 6.2). The bar lies along the axis \(x\) from \(0\) to \(L\) and is fixed to a wall at \(x = 0\). A distributed axial load \(q\), that is a force per unit length of the bar (definition 4.74), and a force \(F\) in the direction of the axis \(x\) at the end \(x = L\) act on it. The cross section that is at the position \(x\) before loading moves along the axis by the displacement \(u(x)\). This displacement is the unknown function: its input is the position \(x\), its output the displacement of the cross section in metres.

The model stands on four assumptions (EP example 3.5.3, p. 148, ONATE1 §2.2, PDF pp. 66-67). For each we say why it holds here, when it does not hold and what it does to the result. The numbers are for the steel bar of the book with length \(10\) m, diameter \(10\) mm and modulus of elasticity \(E = 196\) GPa.

  1. The bar is straight and slender. So a cross section is determined by the single coordinate \(x\) and all quantities are functions of one number. It holds here because the bar is a thousand times longer than it is thick. It does not hold near the ends, where the wall holds the bar or a hook pulls it: there the force is not spread evenly over the cross section and evens out only farther from the end (Saint-Venant's principle, figure 2.16). If we take one diameter for such a region, this is \(10\) mm of \(10\,000\) mm, a thousandth of the length. It also does not hold for a slender bar in compression, because it can bend sideways: in section 3.3.3 we computed that this bar with freely rotating ends bends already at a compressive force of about \(9{,}5\) N.
  2. The load acts along the axis. The force \(F\) and the load \(q\) lie on the axis through the centroids of the cross sections. So the only internal force in a cross section is the axial force \(N\) (definition 2.5), and the bar only stretches or shortens. It does not hold when the force on a part of the bar acts at the distance \(e\) off the axis: then it also bends the bar with a moment of magnitude \(F\,e\), and the stress over the cross section is no longer uniform. By equation (5.25) with the second moment of area of a rectangle \(b\,h^3/12\) (equation (5.18)) the bending part of the stress at the edge of a square cross section of side \(h\) is \(F\,e\,(h/2)/(h^4/12) = (6e/h)\,F/h^2\), that is the fraction \(6e/h\) of the stress \(N/A\). For \(e = 1\) mm and \(h = 10\) mm this is \(60\) %: \(1{,}6\,N/A\) on one side, \(0{,}4\,N/A\) on the other. A millimetre of error in the point of application changes the stress by more than a half.
  3. Cross sections stay plane and perpendicular to the axis. The whole cross section moves by the same \(u(x)\), so the strain \(u'(x)\) is the same over the whole cross section. Why may we assume this? The exact field of the hanging bar from section 1.7.1 (equation (1.19)) has on the axis exactly the displacement of the model, \(a\,(2Lx - x^2)\), and off the axis the cross section bulges by \(0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2)\). At the edge, \(5\) mm from the axis, this is \(0{,}3 \cdot 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1} \cdot (0{,}005\ \text{m})^2 = 1{,}5 \cdot 10^{-12}\) m, thirteen million times less than the displacement of the end, \(19{,}52\) µm. It does not hold at the ends and at a sudden change of cross section, in the same regions as assumption 1.
  4. The stress is uniaxial. On the cut surface only the normal stress \(\sigma = N/A\) acts, the same over the whole cross section (definition 2.6), and the side surface of the bar is free of forces. By definition 3.1 we then have \(\sigma = E\,u'\) and therefore \(N = EA\,u'\). It holds as long as the steel is linearly elastic, for the steel of the book up to the yield stress \(220\) MPa, so for this bar up to the force \(220\ \text{N/mm}^2 \cdot 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2 = 17{,}3\) kN. The area \(A\) is the area before loading, although the bar gets thinner as it stretches: at the force \(10\) kN the strain is \(6{,}5 \cdot 10^{-4}\), the diameter decreases by \(0{,}3 \cdot 6{,}5 \cdot 10^{-4} \cdot 10\ \text{mm} = 1{,}9\) µm and the area by \(0{,}04\) %. The true stress is larger than \(N/A\) by that much.

The product \(EA\) is the axial stiffness. It is a positive function of position, continuous when the cross section changes continuously, and constant for a bar with a constant cross section. When it jumps, as for the bar with a step in section 6.1.4, the definition below no longer suffices, and exactly this will be the reason for the weak form. Equilibrium of parts of the bar gave \(N' + q = 0\) because of the load \(q\) and \(N(L) = F\) because of the force \(F\) (lemma 4.75), and the fixing gave \(u(0) = 0\). Let us write all three requirements as a task about the unknown function \(u\).

Definition 6.1 Strong form of a boundary value problem of a bar (močna oblika robnega problema palice)

The bar lies along the axis \(x\) from \(0\) to \(L\) and is fixed at \(x = 0\). Let the axial stiffness \(EA\) be a positive continuous function on \([0, L]\), the load \(q\) a continuous function on \([0, L]\) (definition 4.74) and \(F\) a number, the force at the end \(x = L\). The strong form (močna oblika) of the boundary value problem of a bar is the task: find a function \(u\) on \([0, L]\) that has a continuous derivative \(u'\) (one-sided at the ends), whose axial force \(N = EA\,u'\) is continuously differentiable on \([0, L]\) and which satisfies

\[\begin{aligned} &\big(EA\,u'\big)'(x) + q(x) = 0 \quad \text{for every } x \in (0, L) , \\ &u(0) = 0 , \qquad EA\,u'(L) = F . \end{aligned} \tag{6.1}\]

Such a statement, an equation at every interior point and conditions at the ends, is a boundary value problem (robni problem).

Source: EP §6.3.6.2 (p. 323, 326-327), COOK §4.7, (4.7-2) (PDF p. 166).

What does the definition say in words? At every point of the bar the derivative of the axial force must equal the negative of the load, so the axial force must change along the bar exactly as the load demands at every metre. For the axial force to have a derivative, the function \(u\) must have a second derivative if \(EA\) is constant. Besides the equation we have two conditions at the ends. The condition \(u(0) = 0\) prescribes a displacement and is an essential condition (bistveni pogoj), the condition \(EA\,u'(L) = N(L) = F\) prescribes a force and is a natural condition (naravni pogoj), as we distinguished them in section 4.4.7 and for the beam in section 5.11.4. In the lectures and in chapter 5 the axial load is denoted \(q_{\mathrm{x}}\), and the equation is the same, \((EA\,u')' + q_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\).

Let us test the definition on the hanging bar (section 4.6.8): \(L = 10\) m, \(EA = 1{,}539 \cdot 10^7\) N, \(q = \rho g A = 6{,}010\) N/m, \(F = 0\). These and all further numbers of the hanging bar are computed from unrounded data (\(E\), \(\rho\), \(g\) and \(A = \pi\,(5\ \text{mm})^2\)), as in chapter 4. With the rounded \(EA\) and \(q\) the last digit can differ: the energy of the true field is \(-391{,}03\) µJ, while the rounded data would give \(-391{,}16\) µJ. Figure 6.3 shows both fields, on axes with the position \(x\) horizontal. The true field \(u = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\) with \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\) has the axial force \(N = EA\,u' = 2a\,EA\,(L - x) = 6{,}010\ \text{N/m} \cdot (L - x)\), which falls from \(60{,}10\) N at the support to zero at the end. Its derivative is \(-6{,}010\) N/m \(= -q\), so the left side of the equation is zero, and \(N(L) = 0 = F\). It satisfies the strong form. The line \(u = c\,x\) from section 4.6.8, however, has the constant axial force \(N = EA\,c\), a horizontal line at a height set by \(c\). Three are drawn, for \(c = aL/2\), \(aL\) and \(3aL/2\), with the forces \(15{,}02\) N, \(30{,}05\) N and \(45{,}07\) N. A horizontal line has no slope, and the equation looks only at the slope of the axial force. So the left side of equation (6.1) is \(0 + q = 6{,}010\) N/m at every point, whatever the number \(c\) is: all three lines give the same line. The strong form of the line therefore does not distinguish better from worse, because the number \(c\) does not appear in it. No line satisfies it, and the measure of how much it fails tells us nothing about the number \(c\).

6.1.2 Three standard cases of a bar (trije standardni primeri palice)

How do we solve the strong form? By two integrations. The first gives the axial force, the second the displacement, each brings one constant number, and the conditions at the ends determine these two numbers. Let us look at three cases that keep returning for a bar (figure 6.4). In all of them the bar is the steel bar of the book with \(L = 10\) m and axial stiffness \(EA = 1{,}539 \cdot 10^7\) N, constant along the length. Each column of the figure shows the bar at the wall at the top, the axial force \(N\) below it and the displacement \(u\) at the bottom, both on axes with the position \(x\) horizontal.

Force at the end. Only the force \(F = 10\) kN at the end acts on the bar, \(q = 0\). This is the bar with a weight from section 4.6.1.

  1. Equation (6.1) is \((EA\,u')' = 0\). A function with zero derivative is constant (corollary 1.86), so \(EA\,u'(x) = C_1\) for some number \(C_1\).
  2. The natural condition \(EA\,u'(L) = F\) gives \(C_1 = F\). The axial force is \(10\) kN everywhere, because every cross section carries the same weight.
  3. Now \(u'(x) = F/(EA)\). The function \(F\,x/(EA)\) has this derivative, and every other one differs from it by a constant number by corollary 1.86: \(u(x) = F\,x/(EA) + C_2\).
  4. The essential condition \(u(0) = 0\) gives \(C_2 = 0\). The displacement is the straight line
    \[u(x) = \frac{F\,x}{EA} , \qquad u(L) = \frac{F\,L}{EA} = \frac{10\,000\ \text{N} \cdot 10\ \text{m}}{1{,}539 \cdot 10^7\ \text{N}} = 6{,}496\ \text{mm} .\]
    The end of the bar moves by \(6{,}496\) mm, as much as the elongation \(F/k\) with \(k = EA/L\) gave in section 4.6.1.

Uniform load. Only the load \(q = 6{,}010\) N/m acts on the bar, the same on every metre, \(F = 0\). This is the hanging bar pulled by its own weight.

  1. The equation is \((EA\,u')' = -q\). The function \(-q\,x\) has this derivative, so \(EA\,u'(x) = -q\,x + C_1\).
  2. The natural condition \(EA\,u'(L) = 0\) gives \(C_1 = q\,L\). The axial force is \(N(x) = q\,(L - x)\) and falls linearly from \(60{,}10\) N at the wall to zero at the end, because every cross section carries the load of the part of the bar between itself and the free end.
  3. Now \(u'(x) = q\,(L - x)/(EA)\). The function \(q\,(L\,x - x^2/2)/(EA)\) has this derivative, so \(u(x) = q\,(L\,x - x^2/2)/(EA) + C_2\).
  4. The essential condition \(u(0) = 0\) gives \(C_2 = 0\). The displacement is the parabola
    \[u(x) = \frac{q}{2EA}\,(2Lx - x^2) = a\,(2Lx - x^2) , \qquad a = \frac{q}{2EA} = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1} .\]
    The end moves by \(a\,L^2 = 19{,}52\) µm, the middle by \(14{,}64\) µm. The graph is steepest at the wall, because the axial force is largest there, and horizontal at the end, because the axial force is zero there.

The equation and both conditions are linear in \(u\), \(q\) and \(F\), so the solutions of the first two cases add. The sum \(u_1 + u_2\) satisfies \((EA\,(u_1 + u_2)')' + q = 0 - q + q = 0\), the condition \(u_1(0) + u_2(0) = 0\) and the condition \(EA\,(u_1 + u_2)'(L) = F + 0\). The bar with a weight and its own weight therefore has the end displacement \(6{,}496\ \text{mm} + 0{,}01952\ \text{mm} = 6{,}516\) mm. The own weight contributes \(0{,}3\) %, which is why we could neglect it in section 4.6.1.

Both ends fixed. The load is the same, \(q = 6{,}010\) N/m, but the end \(x = L\) is fixed to a second wall. Instead of a condition for the force we have there a condition for the displacement, \(u(L) = 0\). The force at the end is now not known. The walls hold the bar with the forces \(R_0\) and \(R_{\mathrm{L}}\), and equilibrium of the whole bar gives a single equation for them, \(R_0 + R_{\mathrm{L}} = q\,L = 60{,}10\) N. One equation does not determine two unknowns. The bar is statically indeterminate (statično nedoločena), like the truss in section 4.7.5, and the displacement gives the missing equation.

  1. As in the previous case, \(EA\,u'(x) = -q\,x + C_1\). The number \(C_1 = N(0)\) is now not known.
  2. The function \((-q\,x^2/2 + C_1\,x)/(EA)\) has the derivative \(u'\), so \(u(x) = (-q\,x^2/2 + C_1\,x)/(EA) + C_2\). The condition \(u(0) = 0\) gives \(C_2 = 0\).
  3. The condition \(u(L) = 0\) gives \(-q\,L^2/2 + C_1\,L = 0\), so \(C_1 = q\,L/2\).
  4. The axial force is \(N(x) = q\,(L/2 - x)\). It falls from \(30{,}05\) N at the left wall to \(-30{,}05\) N at the right one and is zero at the middle. The left half of the bar is in tension, the right half in compression. Each wall carries half of the load: the left one pulls the bar, the right one pushes it, both with a force of magnitude \(30{,}05\) N.
  5. The displacement is the parabola
    \[u(x) = \frac{q}{2EA}\,x\,(L - x) = a\,x\,(L - x) , \qquad u\Big(\frac L2\Big) = \frac{a\,L^2}{4} = 4{,}880\ \text{µm} .\]
    It is zero at both walls and largest at the middle, \(4{,}880\) µm, a quarter of the displacement of the free end in the second case.

Why does each wall carry exactly half? The condition \(u(L) = 0\) says that the integral of the strain \(u' = N/(EA)\) over the bar is zero, so the average axial force is zero. A straight line with slope \(-q\) has zero average exactly when it passes through zero at the middle. As much as the left half stretches, the right half shortens.

The third case also tests assumption 1. The right half is compressed with a force of up to \(30{,}05\) N, which is more than the \(9{,}5\) N at which this bar bends sideways when a constant force compresses it along its whole length and its ends rotate freely (section 3.3.3). Here, however, the compression grows from zero at the middle to \(30{,}05\) N only on the right half, and the left half is in tension and keeps the bar straight. A buckling computation for this distribution of the force gives the critical factor \(1{,}33\) for freely rotating ends and \(5{,}66\) for clamped ends (computed with NumPy): the bar stays straight without guides, with freely rotating ends with a third in reserve. Without the tensioned left half the factor would be \(0{,}80\) and the bar would bend. We had the same two walls for the heated bar in section 3.3.3: there too the force in the bar was determined not by equilibrium but by the condition that the ends do not move. The third case is not a task of definition 6.1, because at the end \(x = L\) it has an essential condition instead of a natural one. The equation in the interior is the same. In the rest of the chapter we stay with the bar with a free end.

Let us return to the hanging bar and to the question of what the strong form says about an approximation. The line \(u = c\,x\) did not satisfy it for any \(c\). The next form will ask less of the function.

6.1.3 Weak form of a bar (šibka oblika palice)

Theorem 4.76 showed that the true displacement satisfies an equation with integrals over the bar in which only the first derivative of the displacement appears. This equation is equilibrium multiplied by a virtual displacement and integrated over the bar. Now let us take it as the definition of the task. We keep in mind that we shall assemble trial fields from pieces, so we allow functions with kinks (pregib), such as the field with a roof in section 1.15.5. The displacement of such a field is continuous, but its derivative may jump at finitely many points. The next section treats these functions exactly, here we say only what we need.

Definition 6.2 Weak form of a boundary value problem of a bar (šibka oblika robnega problema palice)

The bar lies along the axis \(x\) from \(0\) to \(L\) and is fixed at \(x = 0\). Let the axial stiffness \(EA\) (positive) and the load \(q\) be functions continuous piece by piece: there is a partition of the interval \([0, L]\) for which both are continuous on every closed piece, with one-sided values at the ends. Let the force at the end \(x = L\) be \(F\). An admissible function of a bar (dopustna funkcija palice) is a function \(w\) on \([0, L]\) that is continuous, satisfies \(w(0) = 0\), and for which there is a partition \(0 = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_{\mathrm{m}} = L\) for which \(w\) is differentiable on every closed piece \([x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}}]\) with a continuous derivative, one-sided at the ends. The derivative \(w'\) is thus determined everywhere except at the points of the partition, and the integral of a product with a function continuous on pieces means the sum of the integrals over the pieces. For several functions we take a partition that is common to all, adding to it the points of the partitions of the other functions. The weak form (šibka oblika) of the boundary value problem of a bar is the task: find an admissible function \(u\) that for every admissible function \(w\) satisfies

\[\int_0^L EA\,u'\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L q\,w\,\mathrm{d}x + F\,w(L) . \tag{6.2}\]

The admissible function \(w\) is here called a test function (preizkusna funkcija).

Source: EP §6.3.6.2, (6.3.40) to (6.3.43) (p. 327), COOK §4.1 (PDF p. 150) and §4.7 (PDF p. 166), BOWER §8.1.2 (PDF p. 496). Summarized from theorem 4.76, the notation with pieces is not from the sources.

The test function is the virtual displacement from section 4.4: an imagined change of displacement that does not move the support (definition 4.70). The condition \(w(0) = 0\) is this constraint, just as for the bar. The function \(u\) in the task is an admissible function, so it satisfies the same condition and the same continuity as the test functions, but not the other equation. The weak form asks for a single derivative of the displacement, \(u'\), whereas the strong form also asks for the derivative of the axial force, that is \(u''\) for a constant stiffness. The natural condition \(EA\,u'(L) = F\) is built into the weak form: the term \(F\,w(L)\) stands right on the right side of equation (6.2). The essential condition \(u(0) = 0\) is not in the equation, because it is part of the set of admissible functions. Figure 6.5 compares the requirements. At the top is the bar, fixed to the wall at \(x = 0\), with the load \(q\) shown by the arrows and five chosen points. The strong form asks for the equilibrium \(N'(x) + q(x) = 0\) at every point of the bar, not only at the five drawn. Below is the weak form: the area under the product \(N\,w'\) must be equal to the area under the product \(q\,w\), where the axes end at the length \(L\) of the bar. Figure 6.6 shows two test functions. The first is smooth, the second has a kink at \(x = L/2\), so its derivative \(w'\) jumps there from \(1\) to \(0\), as the filled and open circle below the kink show. Both are zero at the fixed end. Each is drawn on axes, \(w\) above and its derivative \(w'\) below it. The second is a roof of two straight pieces, the first with slope \(1\), the second with slope \(0\).

How are the forms related? If \(u\) is a solution of the strong form, it is a solution of the weak form. The converse holds under a condition that we state in the theorem, and from the weak form follow all the conditions of the strong one, even those that are not in its statement.

We follow the proof on figure 6.7. At the top is the bar at the wall, divided by the points of the partition into pieces. Integration by parts on every piece leaves terms at the ends of the piece: two at the junction \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\), one from piece \(k\) and one from piece \(k+1\), one at the end and none at the support, because every test function is zero there. Below, on axes, are three test functions with which the second direction of the proof extracts one condition each from a single equation. The bump \(\psi\), nonzero only on one piece, leaves the equation of equilibrium on that piece. The roof \(t_{\mathrm{k}}\), which reaches \(h\) to each side of the junction, leaves the jump of the axial force at the junction. The line \(w = x\) leaves the condition at the end.

Theorem 6.3 Strong and weak form of a bar (močna in šibka oblika palice)

Let the bar, \(EA\), \(q\) and \(F\) be as in definition 6.2.

  1. Let \(EA\) and \(q\) be continuous on \([0, L]\). If \(u\) is a solution of the strong form (definition 6.1), then \(u\) is a solution of the weak form.
  2. Let \(u\) be a solution of the weak form and let there be a partition \(0 = x_0 < \dots < x_{\mathrm{m}} = L\) for which \(EA\) and \(q\) are continuous on every closed piece \([x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}}]\), \(u\) is differentiable on every piece with a continuous derivative, and on every piece the axial force \(EA\,u'\) equals a function \(N_{\mathrm{k}}\) that is continuously differentiable on the closed piece. Then:
    • (a) \(N_{\mathrm{k}}'(x) + q_{\mathrm{k}}(x) = 0\) for every \(x \in [x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}}]\) and every \(k = 1, \dots, m\), where \(q_{\mathrm{k}}\) is the continuous function on the closed piece that equals \(q\) on the open piece,
    • (b) \(N_{\mathrm{k}}(x_{\mathrm{k}}) = N_{\mathrm{k}+1}(x_{\mathrm{k}})\) for \(k = 1, \dots, m-1\), so the axial force is continuous across the points of the partition,
    • (c) \(N_{\mathrm{m}}(L) = F\).
Proof

We must show two directions. The first is integration by parts on the pieces, the second reverses this step and from the equation for every test function chooses in turn functions that are nonzero only on one piece, at one junction and at the end.

1. The strong form implies the weak form.

  1. The derivative \(u'\) is continuous on \([0, L]\), so \(u\) is differentiable on \([0, L]\), one-sidedly at the ends, and therefore continuous (lemma 1.80). Together with \(u(0) = 0\) this is an admissible function with a partition of one piece.
  2. Let \(w\) be an admissible function with the partition \(0 = x_0 < \dots < x_{\mathrm{m}} = L\). By definition 6.1 the axial force \(N = EA\,u'\) is continuously differentiable on \([0, L]\), and the field \(w\) is differentiable on every closed piece with a continuous derivative. By corollary 3.56 on integration by parts, on the piece \([x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}}]\) we have
    \[\int_{\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{k}-1}}^{x_{\mathrm{k}}} N\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x = N(x_{\mathrm{k}})\,w(x_{\mathrm{k}}) - N(x_{\mathrm{k}-1})\,w(x_{\mathrm{k}-1}) - \int_{\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{k}-1}}^{x_{\mathrm{k}}} N'\,w\,\mathrm{d}x .\]
  3. We add over \(k\). By the convention of definition 6.2, \(\int_0^L N\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x\) is the sum of the integrals over the pieces, so it is the sum of the left sides. The function \(N'\,w = -q\,w\) is continuous on \([0, L]\), so the sum of the integrals \(\int_{\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{k}-1}}^{x_{\mathrm{k}}} N'\,w\,\mathrm{d}x\) equals \(\int_0^L N'\,w\,\mathrm{d}x\) by additivity of the integral (lemma 3.54, item 2). At the point \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\) for \(1 \le k \le m-1\) there appear the terms \(N(x_{\mathrm{k}})\,w(x_{\mathrm{k}})\) from piece \(k\) and \(-N(x_{\mathrm{k}})\,w(x_{\mathrm{k}})\) from piece \(k+1\). They are the same number, because \(N\) and \(w\) are continuous, so they cancel. What remains is
    \[\int_0^L N\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x = N(L)\,w(L) - N(0)\,w(0) - \int_0^L N'\,w\,\mathrm{d}x .\]
  4. Since \(w(0) = 0\), \(N(L) = F\) and \(N' = -q\) by equation (6.1), this is \(\int_0^L N\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x = F\,w(L) + \int_0^L q\,w\,\mathrm{d}x\). Because \(N = EA\,u'\), this is equation (6.2).

2. The weak form implies the conditions.

The three test functions in figure 6.9 are all zero at the support. The bar lies along the axis \(x\) from \(0\) to \(L\). The first is a bump \(\psi\) on one piece and zero elsewhere. The second is a roof with its peak \(1\) at \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\) and half-width \(h\), zero outside it. The third is the straight line \(w = x\).

  1. Let \(w\) be an admissible function. The normal force \(N\) on the bar is continuous on each piece, its graph has three pieces, it jumps at the partition points, and at the end it equals \(N_{\mathrm{m}}(L)\), which need not be \(F\). We refine the partition with the partition of the function \(w\). At the added points \(N\) and \(w\) are continuous, so their terms cancel in the summation, as in step 3 of the first direction. By corollary 3.56 on every piece and after summation we have
    \[\begin{aligned} \int_0^L EA\,u'\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x &= N_{\mathrm{m}}(L)\,w(L) \\ &\quad + \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{m-1} \big(N_{\mathrm{k}}(x_{\mathrm{k}}) - N_{\mathrm{k}+1}(x_{\mathrm{k}})\big)\,w(x_{\mathrm{k}}) - \int_0^L N'\,w\,\mathrm{d}x , \end{aligned}\]
    where \(N'\) on piece \(k\) is the derivative of the function \(N_{\mathrm{k}}\), and the term at \(x = 0\) vanishes because of \(w(0) = 0\).
  2. Let us introduce \(J_{\mathrm{k}} = N_{\mathrm{k}}(x_{\mathrm{k}}) - N_{\mathrm{k}+1}(x_{\mathrm{k}})\), the jump of the axial force at the point \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\). We insert this into equation (6.2) and move all terms to the left side:
    \[\begin{aligned} &\big(N_{\mathrm{m}}(L) - F\big)\,w(L) + \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{m-1} J_{\mathrm{k}}\,w(x_{\mathrm{k}}) - \int_0^L \big(N' + q\big)\,w\,\mathrm{d}x = 0 \\ &\text{for every admissible function } w . \quad (*) \end{aligned}\]
  3. Let us choose a piece \([x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}}]\) and a function \(\psi\) that is differentiable on it with a continuous derivative and satisfies \(\psi(x_{\mathrm{k}-1}) = \psi(x_{\mathrm{k}}) = 0\). The function \(w\) that equals \(\psi\) on this piece and zero elsewhere is continuous, zero at \(x = 0\) and differentiable with a continuous derivative on every closed piece of the partition, so it is admissible. It is also zero at all points of the partition. Equation \((*)\) therefore says \(\int_{\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{k}-1}}^{x_{\mathrm{k}}} (N_{\mathrm{k}}' + q)\,\psi\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\) for every such \(\psi\).
  4. The function \(N_{\mathrm{k}}' + q_{\mathrm{k}}\) is continuous on \([x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}}]\), because \(N_{\mathrm{k}}\) is continuously differentiable and \(q_{\mathrm{k}}\) continuous on the closed piece. By the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations (lemma 4.77) we therefore have \(N_{\mathrm{k}}' + q_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\) on the whole piece, since \(q_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(q\) agree on the open piece, where we integrate. The lemma argues like this. Choose a point \(x^*\) on the axis \(x\). If the function \(N_{\mathrm{k}}' + q_{\mathrm{k}}\) were positive there, by continuity it would be positive on a band around \(x^*\), and a bump \(\psi\) that is positive only on this band would give an integral of the product greater than zero, not zero. For a negative value the argument is the same with \(-\psi\). This is item (a).
  5. Now the integral in \((*)\) is zero for every admissible function \(w\), and what remains is \((N_{\mathrm{m}}(L) - F)\,w(L) + \sum_{\mathrm{k}} J_{\mathrm{k}}\,w(x_{\mathrm{k}}) = 0\), the term at the end and the terms at the junctions.
  6. Let \(1 \le k \le m-1\) and \(0 < h < \min(x_{\mathrm{k}} - x_{\mathrm{k}-1},\, x_{\mathrm{k}+1} - x_{\mathrm{k}})\). The roof \(t_{\mathrm{k}}\), which is zero to the left of \(x_{\mathrm{k}} - h\) and to the right of \(x_{\mathrm{k}} + h\), rises linearly to \(1\) at \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\) and falls linearly, is continuous, zero at \(0\) and \(L\), and differentiable with a continuous derivative on every piece of the partition refined by the points \(x_{\mathrm{k}} \pm h\). It is therefore admissible. Its value is \(1\) at \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(0\) at all other points of the partition, including \(L\). Step 5 gives \(J_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\). This is item (b).
  7. The function \(w(x) = x\) with \(w(L) = L\) is also admissible. Since all \(J_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\) by step 6, step 5 gives \((N_{\mathrm{m}}(L) - F)\,L = 0\) and therefore \(N_{\mathrm{m}}(L) = F\). This is item (c).

Source: The proof is not from a source. The connection between the two forms for a smooth case is mentioned by EP §6.3.6.2 (pp. 323-328) and COOK §4.7 (PDF pp. 166-167), theorem 4.78 is the same conclusion for a continuously differentiable axial force.

What did the theorem show? The first direction is integration by parts, which moves the derivative from the axial force to the test function, as in theorem 4.76, except that we run it piece by piece also across the points where the test function has a kink. The second direction says more than it seems at first sight. From the single equation (6.2) for all admissible functions \(w\) we get the equation of equilibrium on every piece, the natural condition \(N(L) = F\) and the continuity of the axial force across every point where a piece ends. This continuity is not written in the equation, yet the equation demands it.

Why can we leave the condition for the force to the equation, but not the condition for the displacement? A test function may move the free end, like the line \(w = x\) with \(w(L) = L\). The force \(F\) at the end therefore does the virtual work \(F\,w(L)\), the equation weighs it and demands \(N(L) = F\). At the support, however, every test function is zero. The force of the wall does no virtual work, so the equation does not see it and cannot say where this end stands. The condition \(u(0) = 0\) must therefore be demanded separately, in the set of admissible functions.

For the hanging bar with the line the difference now shows. The line \(u = c\,x\) is an admissible function. Into equation (6.2) we insert the test function \(w = x\) from figure 6.6. The left side is \(\int_0^L EA\,c\,\mathrm{d}x = EA\,c\,L\), the right side \(\int_0^L q\,x\,\mathrm{d}x = q\,L^2/2\), and the equality gives \(c = q\,L/(2EA) = a L = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\). This is exactly the equation from step 4 of the first trial field in section 4.6.8. The strong form gave nothing, because the number \(c\) dropped out, and the weak form determined it, because it asked of the trial field only an average, equilibrium with the weight \(w\). The line does not satisfy the equation for every test function, because it is not the true field. With \(w = x^2/(1\ \text{m})\), that is \(w' = 2x/(1\ \text{m})\) with \(x\) in metres, the left side is the area under the line \(EA\,c\,w'\), \(\int_0^L EA\,c\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x = EA\,c\,L^2/(1\ \text{m}) = 3005\) N m, and the right side the area under the parabola \(q\,w\), \(\int_0^L q\,w\,\mathrm{d}x = q\,L^3/3\,(1\ \text{m})^{-1} = 2003\) N m. The true field \(a\,(2Lx - x^2)\) gives on the left the area under \(N\,w'\), which is the same as on the right, \(2003\) N m. The line therefore satisfies the equation only for the chosen test function, not for all, and this is what we expect of it: a trial field with one free number satisfies one requirement. The idea that a trial field with \(n\) free numbers satisfies \(n\) requirements we develop in the following sections.

6.1.4 A bar with a step (palica s stopnico)

What happens if the cross section of a bar changes suddenly along its length? Take a steel hanging bar with an upper half, \(5\) m long, of diameter \(10\) mm and cross-sectional area \(A = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\), and a lower half, \(5\) m long, of diameter \(5\) mm and area \(A/4 = 19{,}63\ \text{mm}^2\) (figure 6.11). The upper end is fixed, the lower end free, we measure the position \(x\) from the support downward, \(F = 0\), the only load is the weight. The material is the steel of the book (\(E = 196\) GPa, \(\rho = 7800\ \text{kg/m}^3\), \(g = 9{,}81\ \text{m/s}^2\)). The load per unit length is \(q = \rho g A = 6{,}010\) N/m above and \(\rho g A/4 = 1{,}502\) N/m below. The step is a simplification: a real step would have a rounded transition, and the one-dimensional model does not capture the stress concentration next to it. What does this cost? If we take one diameter of the thicker part for the region of the transition, \(10\) mm of \(10\,000\) mm, and the strain there were even twice the computed \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\), the displacement of the end would change by at most \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} \cdot 10\ \text{mm} = 0{,}02\) µm of \(12{,}20\) µm, that is by \(0{,}16\) %. For the displacement the step is a good simplification, for the largest stress at the transition it is not. We deal with stress concentration, for the example of a hole in a plate, in chapter 11.

First let us find the true displacement by the method of chapter 4, piece by piece. Equilibrium of the part of the bar below a cross section (lemma 4.75) gives \(N(x) = \rho g\,(A/4)\,(10 - x)\) in the lower half, with \(x\) in metres, and \(N(x) = \rho g\,(A/4) \cdot 5 + \rho g A\,(5 - x)\) in the upper one. At \(x = 5\) m both expressions equal \(7{,}512\) N, so the axial force is continuous, and at \(x = 0\) we have \(N = 37{,}56\) N, the weight of the whole bar, \(5 \cdot 6{,}010 + 5 \cdot 1{,}502\) N. The strain \(u' = N/(EA)\) has the value \(4{,}880 \cdot 10^{-7}\) above the step and \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\) below. They meet at the same point, but the derivative of the displacement jumps by a factor of \(4\), the ratio of the areas: the same force in a cross section four times thinner gives four times the elongation. We get the displacement from the integral of the strain: \(u(5\ \text{m}) = 7{,}320\) µm and \(u(10\ \text{m}) = 12{,}20\) µm. The graph of the displacement therefore has a kink at the point \(x = 5\) m and there is no second derivative there. The figure shows each of the three quantities on its own axes, with a different scale.

What does the strong form say about such a field? Its equation \((EA\,u')' + q = 0\) requires \(EA\) to be continuous (definition 6.1), but the axial stiffness jumps by a factor of \(4\) at the step. The load \(q\) also jumps, from \(6{,}010\) to \(1{,}502\) N/m, and so the axial force \(N' = -q\) does not have a continuous derivative across the step. This definition does not capture the true field. We would have to split the strong form into two parts and add two more conditions at the step: the displacement is continuous, the axial force is continuous. These two conditions are not written in the equation.

The weak form needs nothing extra. Let us test it. With \(w = x\) the left side of equation (6.2) is \(\int_0^L N\,\mathrm{d}x = 131{,}46\) N m, the whole area under the axial force, \(112{,}68 + 18{,}78\) N m, and the right side is \(\int_0^5 6{,}010\,x\,\mathrm{d}x + \int_5^{10} 1{,}502\,x\,\mathrm{d}x = 131{,}46\) N m. The equality also holds for the test function with a kink from figure 6.6, here with the kink at \(x = 5\) m, \(w = x\) up to \(5\) m and \(w = 5\) m afterwards: the left side is \(\int_0^5 N\,\mathrm{d}x = 112{,}68\) N m, only the area above the step, because \(w' = 0\) below it, the right side \(\int_0^5 6{,}010\,x\,\mathrm{d}x + \int_5^{10} 1{,}502 \cdot 5\,\mathrm{d}x = 112{,}68\) N m. The displacement of the bar with a step is an admissible function and a solution of the weak form for every test function, even though its derivative is discontinuous. This follows from steps 2 to 4 of the first direction of the proof of theorem 6.3: we take the partition common with the point \(x = 5\) m, the axial force is continuous and \(N' = -q\) on every piece, the integral \(\int N'\,w\) is a sum over the pieces, because \(q\) jumps at \(x = 5\) m, and the terms at the step cancel. Theorem 6.3, item 2, says the converse: every solution of the weak form with piecewise smooth fields \(u\) and \(N\) has a continuous axial force and a continuous displacement at the step, even though we wrote this nowhere. The continuity of the displacement is in the definition of an admissible function, and the continuity of the axial force came out of the equation itself. This is the reason why the weak form also admits bars whose stiffness or load jumps.

What if the test function is not continuous? Take \(w = x\) up to \(5\) m and \(w = 5{,}5\) m afterwards. It differs from the function with a kink only in that at \(x = 5\) m it jumps by \(0{,}5\) m (figure 6.12). Both functions are drawn on axes \(x\) and \(w\). It satisfies \(w(0) = 0\) and is differentiable with a continuous derivative on every closed piece, but it is not continuous, so it is not an admissible function. We test the requirement of continuity on the true displacement of the bar with a step. If we did not demand it, equation (6.2) would have to hold for this function too.

  1. On both pieces the derivative is the same as for the function with a kink, \(1\) and \(0\), because the derivative does not register the jump. The left side is therefore still \(\int_0^5 N\,\mathrm{d}x = 112{,}68\) N m, the area above the step.
  2. The right side, \(\int_0^5 6{,}010\,x\,\mathrm{d}x + \int_5^{10} 1{,}502 \cdot 5{,}5\,\mathrm{d}x\), is larger than for the function with a kink by \(\int_5^{10} 1{,}502 \cdot 0{,}5\,\mathrm{d}x = 3{,}76\) N m, so it is \(116{,}44\) N m. The load \(1{,}502\) N/m on the lower \(5\) m acts at a higher value of \(w\), and the left side does not see this height.
  3. The two sides do not agree, \(112{,}68 \ne 116{,}44\). The true displacement would violate the equation for this function, even though it is a solution.

The excess \(3{,}76\) N m is the axial force at the step \(N(5) = 7{,}512\) N multiplied by the jump \(0{,}5\) m. For a jump \(s\) the excess is \(7{,}512\,s\) N m, zero only for \(s = 0\). The continuity of the function \(w\) in the definition of an admissible function is therefore not an add-on: only with it do the left side, which sees only the derivative, and the right side, which sees the value, measure the same function.

6.1.5 Weak form of a beam (šibka oblika nosilca)

We put the same question to the beam from chapter 5. Let it lie along the axis \(x\) from \(0\) to \(L\) with bending stiffness \(EI\) and load \(q\), positive upward. The strong form follows from the relations between the load and the internal forces (corollary 5.11, \(V' + q = 0\) and \(M' + V = 0\)) and from \(M = EI\,v''\) (equation (5.24)): it is the equation

\[\big(EI\,v''\big)'' = q\]

with four conditions at the ends from section 5.7.2. At every end there is one condition from the pair \((v, V)\) and one from the pair \((v', M)\): essential if the support prescribes the deflection or the slope, natural if it prescribes the shear force or the moment (the table in section 5.11.4). For a constant stiffness the equation reduces to the equation of the deflection curve \(EI\,v'''' = q\) (theorem 5.42) and \(v\) must have four derivatives.

We know the weak form from theorem 5.63: equilibrium multiplied by a virtual displacement \(w\) and integrated by parts twice. With virtual displacements that have \(\delta u = 0\) the axial part drops out (in the linear theory it is handled by the weak form of the bar), and with \(M = EI\,v''\) what remains is

\[\begin{aligned} \int_0^L EI\,v''\,w''\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^L q\,w\,\mathrm{d}x &+ \Big[F_{\mathrm{y}}\,w + M_0\,w'\Big]_{\mathrm{x} = \mathrm{L}} \\ &+ \Big[F_{\mathrm{y}}\,w + M_0\,w'\Big]_{\mathrm{x} = 0} . \end{aligned} \tag{6.3}\]

Here \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(M_0\) are the force across the axis and the moment of a couple at the ends (each end has its own values, the loads are positive upward and counterclockwise), and at every end we omit the terms of the components that the support forbids. The test functions \(w\) are the virtual displacements of a beam (definition 5.61): \(w\) and \(w'\) continuous, \(w''\) continuous (the next section allows \(w''\) to have jumps), and \(w = 0\) where \(v\) is prescribed and \(w' = 0\) where \(v'\) is prescribed. We proved the equivalence of the two forms in chapter 5: the weak one follows from the strong one by theorem 5.63, and the converse by theorem 5.66, which gives the equation \((EI\,v'')'' = q\) in the interior and the natural conditions \(V(L) = F_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(M(L) = M_0\) at a free end \(x = L\) and \(-V(0) = F_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(-M(0) = M_0\) at a free end \(x = 0\). A point force or a couple in the interior adds a term by corollary 5.65. The natural conditions and the point forces are therefore in the weak form only terms on the right side.

Why is the continuity of the slope \(w'\) important here? The equation contains \(w''\), and if \(w'\) had a jump \(s\), the integral by pieces would drop the term \(M\,s\) at that point, and the true deflection would not satisfy the equation (as for the bar with a jump of the function \(w\), see corollary 6.14, the paragraph after the proof). The term \(M_0\,w'\) at a free end is the work of the couple on the rotation of the end, which must be well defined. Later in this chapter we show with numbers that the energy of a rounded kink in the deflection grows beyond all bounds when we shorten the rounding.

Let us test equation (6.3) on the cantilever from section 5.1.3: \(L = 1\) m, force \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = -500\) N at the free end, \(M_0 = 0\), clamped at \(x = 0\). The moment is \(M = EI\,v'' = -500\ \text{N} \cdot (L - x)\). The test function must have \(w(0) = w'(0) = 0\), so \(w = x^2/(1\ \text{m})\) is one of the admissible ones, with \(x\) in metres, \(w'' = 2/(1\ \text{m})\) and \(w(L) = 1\) m. The left side is \(\int_0^L M\,w''\,\mathrm{d}x = -500\ \text{N m}\), the right side \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\,w(L) + M_0\,w'(L) = -500\ \text{N} \cdot 1\ \text{m} = -500\ \text{N m}\). The equation holds. We do the same on the simply supported beam from section 5.1.3, \(L = 2\) m, \(q = -q_0\) with \(q_0 = 1\) kN/m, where \(M = \tfrac12\,q_0\,x\,(L - x)\). The test function \(w = x\,(L - x)/(1\ \text{m})\) is zero at both supports, and \(w'' = -2/(1\ \text{m})\). The left side is \(\int_0^L M\,w''\,\mathrm{d}x = -1333{,}3\) N m, the right side \(\int_0^L q\,w\,\mathrm{d}x = -1333{,}3\) N m, there are no terms at the ends, because \(w = 0\) at both supports and \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = M_0 = 0\).

The support says what the trial field must satisfy. A beam clamped at \(x = 0\) requires \(v(0) = 0\) and \(v'(0) = 0\). A simply supported beam requires \(v = 0\) at both supports, but the trial field does not require the moment \(M = 0\), because it is a natural condition and equation (6.3) satisfies it by itself when the field is the true one, as we saw in section 5.11.4.

6.1.6 Weak form of a body (šibka oblika telesa)

The last answer is for a body. Take the body from section 4.5.1: a set of points \(V\), the surface divided into a part \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) with prescribed displacement \(\bar{\vek u}\) and a part \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) with prescribed force per unit area \(\bar{\vek t}\), and the body force \(\vek b\). The strong form gathers what we established in chapters 1 to 3: the equilibrium equations \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} \partial\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}} + b_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\) in the interior, the condition \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \bar{\vek t}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\), the condition \(\vek u = \bar{\vek u}\) on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), the stress from the strain by the general Hooke's law (definition 3.25) and the strain from the displacement (definition 1.121). The weak form is the equality of internal and external virtual work, equation (4.52), in which the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is expressed by the displacement \(\vek u\). The equivalence of the two forms is already proved. From the equilibrium equations and the condition on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) the equation of virtual work follows by theorem 4.82, and from the equation of virtual work for every admissible virtual displacement the equilibrium equations and the condition on \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) follow by theorem 4.84. The condition on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is built into the set of fields in both. The theorems hold under the assumptions of section 4.5.1: a body made of boxes, a continuously differentiable and symmetric stress. Plane states, in which two coordinates suffice, have the same form and we treat them in chapter 11.

The test function is here a kinematically admissible virtual displacement (figure 6.16): the body is with its left face glued to the wall, where \(\vek w = \vek 0\), and with the distance from the wall the displacement \(\vek w\) grows, as the dashed outline of the moved body shows. On the rest of the surface \(S_{\mathrm{t}}\) the displacement is not prescribed. The axes show the directions \(x\) and \(z\). Let us test this on the cube of section 4.5.1, glued to the table, \(h = 10\) mm, \(\tau_0 = 50\) MPa, the stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}} = \tau_0\) everywhere. The virtual displacement \(\vek w = (\gamma\,z, 0, 0)\) with \(\gamma = 0{,}001\) is admissible, because it is zero at \(z = 0\) (section 4.5.2), and has \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}(\vek w) = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}}(\vek w) = \gamma/2\), the other virtual strains are zero. The internal virtual work is \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} (\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{zx}})\,\gamma/2\,\mathrm{d}V = \tau_0\,\gamma\,h^3 = 0{,}0500\) N m. We neglect the weight, \(\vek b = \vek 0\), as in section 4.5.1. For this \(\vek w\) this costs nothing: the weight is vertical and \(\vek w\) horizontal, so \(\vek b\cdot\vek w = 0\), and the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) that the weight adds is multiplied by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}(\vek w) = 0\). The external virtual work comes only from the top face with \(\bar{\vek t} = \tau_0\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), where \(w_{\mathrm{x}} = \gamma h\): \(\tau_0\,\gamma\,h \cdot h^2 = 0{,}0500\) N m. The front and the back face are free, \(\bar{\vek t} = \vek 0\). On the left and right faces the forces are vertical, \(w_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), and their work is zero, and the bottom face is \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), where \(\vek w = \vek 0\). The equality holds.

We draw the bilinear form as a machine \(B\) with two inputs, because it needs two fields, and one output, the number \(B(u, w)\). If we split the first input into \(\alpha u_1 + \beta u_2\), the output splits into a sum of two outputs, and the same holds for the second input. The linear form is a machine \(\ell\) with one input and one output, which splits in the same way. For a symmetric form swapping the inputs does not change the output.

All three statements have the same form. On the left is an expression that is linear in the unknown field for a fixed test function and linear in the test function for a fixed field, and on the right an expression that is linear only in the test function and contains the loads. Let us name them.

Definition 6.4 Bilinear form (bilinearna forma)

Let \(W\) be a vector space of functions or fields (definition 1.16). A bilinear form (bilinearna forma) on \(W\) is a function \(B\) that takes two elements \(u\) and \(w\) of the space \(W\) as input and gives one number \(B(u, w)\) as output, and is linear in each argument separately: \(B(\alpha u_1 + \beta u_2, w) = \alpha\,B(u_1, w) + \beta\,B(u_2, w)\) and \(B(u, \alpha w_1 + \beta w_2) = \alpha\,B(u, w_1) + \beta\,B(u, w_2)\) for all \(u, u_1, u_2, w, w_1, w_2 \in W\) and numbers \(\alpha, \beta\). It is symmetric (simetrična) if \(B(u, w) = B(w, u)\) for all \(u, w \in W\).

Source: EP §6.2.4 (pp. 281-282), (6.2.31).

Definition 6.5 Linear form (linearna forma)

Let \(W\) be a vector space of functions or fields. A linear form (linearna forma) on \(W\) is a function \(\ell\) that takes an element \(w\) of the space \(W\) as input and gives a number \(\ell(w)\) as output, and satisfies \(\ell(\alpha w_1 + \beta w_2) = \alpha\,\ell(w_1) + \beta\,\ell(w_2)\) for all \(w_1, w_2 \in W\) and numbers \(\alpha, \beta\).

Source: EP §6.2.4 (p. 281), §6.3.6.2, (6.3.42) (p. 327).

The notation \(\ell(w)\) with a function in brackets is a linear form. The letter \(\ell\) is in chapter 2 the lever arm, in chapter 1 the length of a small piece, and \(\ell(t)\) is the secant line in the proof of theorem 1.85. Here \(\ell(w)\) with a test function in brackets means a linear form. The three tasks that we have collected are, in these notations:

task \(B(u, w)\) \(\ell(w)\)
bar \(\int_0^L EA\,u'\,w'\,\mathrm{d}x\) \(\int_0^L q\,w\,\mathrm{d}x + F\,w(L)\)
beam \(\int_0^L EI\,u''\,w''\,\mathrm{d}x\) \(\int_0^L q\,w\,\mathrm{d}x + [F_{\mathrm{y}} w + M_0 w']_{\mathrm{x} = \mathrm{L}} + [F_{\mathrm{y}} w + M_0 w']_{\mathrm{x} = 0}\)
body \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} \sum_{\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j},\mathrm{k},\mathrm{l}} C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}}(\vek u)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}(\vek w)\,\mathrm{d}V\) \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} \vek b\cdot\vek w\,\mathrm{d}V + \int_{\mathrm{S}_\mathrm{t}} \bar{\vek t}\cdot\vek w\,\mathrm{d}A\)

In the column bar we get from \(u\) the derivative \(u'\) and from \(w\) the derivative \(w'\), and \(B\) is their product with the stiffness. For the beam these are the second derivatives, for the body the strains of both fields, connected by the constants \(C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\). The arrows across the middle show that swapping the fields gives the same product.

For a body \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}}(\vek u)\) is the strain of the field \(\vek u\) (equation (1.59)), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}(\vek w)\) the strain of the test field \(\vek w\), which is a kinematically admissible virtual displacement (definition 4.79), and \(C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\) the constants of the generalized Hooke's law (definition 3.25), so that \(\sum_{\mathrm{k},\mathrm{l}} C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{kl}}(\vek u) = \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}\). Each of the three has the first argument linear because in every case the stress quantity is linear in the displacement (the general Hooke's law, definition 3.25, with equation (1.59) for the body, \(N = EA\,u'\) and \(M = EI\,v''\) by equation (5.24) for the bar and the beam), and the second because the virtual strain and the virtual displacement appear linearly. Symmetry: for the bar and the beam the product of functions is symmetric, for the body \(C_{\mathrm{ijkl}} = C_{\mathrm{klij}}\) by theorem 3.62, item 1, and the change of the order of the arguments is an exchange of the indices of a pair. All three tasks therefore have the same form.

For \(B(x, x^2)\) we take \(u = x\) and \(w = x^2\). The area under the curve \(u'\,w' = 2x\) is \(1\), the area under the curve \(u'\,w = x^2\) is \(\tfrac13\), together \(\tfrac43\). After the swap the first term is the same and the second is \(2x \cdot x = 2x^2\) with area \(\tfrac23\), together \(\tfrac53\).

Symmetry is not self-evident. On functions on \([0, 1]\) take \(B(u, w) = \int_0^1 (u'\,w' + u'\,w)\,\mathrm{d}x\). It is bilinear, because \(u'\,w'\) and \(u'\,w\) are linear in \(u\) and in \(w\) separately. For \(u = x\) and \(w = x^2\) we have \(B(x, x^2) = \int_0^1 (2x + x^2)\,\mathrm{d}x = 1 + \tfrac13 = \tfrac43\). If we swap the arguments, \(B(x^2, x) = \int_0^1 (2x + 2x^2)\,\mathrm{d}x = 1 + \tfrac23 = \tfrac53\). The numbers differ, so \(B\) is not symmetric. The cause is the term \(u'\,w\): the derivative stands at the first function, the value at the second, and after the swap this is no longer the same product. In the table, in each task the same quantities stand in both places, the derivatives \(u'\) and \(w'\) for the bar, \(u''\) and \(w''\) for the beam, or the strain with the constants \(C_{\mathrm{ijkl}}\) for the body, so these forms are symmetric. This property will be a condition of theorem 6.44.

On the \(x\) axis we sample the derivatives \(u'\) and \(w'\) at points \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\) with spacing \(\Delta x\), as two rows of columns. Every rectangle \(EA\,u'_{\mathrm{i}}\,w'_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta x\) is one term of the inner product. As \(\Delta x\) decreases, the stepped curve approaches the smooth curve \(2x\), with area \(1\) under it, which is \(B(x, x^2)\). If we take the same field on both sides, every term is a square and so never negative.

A second view of the bilinear form of the bar: as an inner product. We sample the derivatives \(u'\) and \(w'\) at points \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\) with spacing \(\Delta x\), which gives vectors of numbers \(u'_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(w'_{\mathrm{i}}\). The sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} EA\,u'_{\mathrm{i}}\,w'_{\mathrm{i}}\,\Delta x\) is the inner product of these vectors (definition 2.8) with the weight \(EA\,\Delta x\), and the integral is its limit as \(\Delta x \to 0\). For \(EA = 1\) and \(u = x\), \(w = x^2\) on \([0, 1]\) we have \(B(x, x^2) = \int_0^1 1 \cdot 2x\,\mathrm{d}x = 1\). So, for \(EA > 0\), \(B\) has the properties of an inner product: it is symmetric, and \(B(w, w) = \int_0^1 EA\,(w')^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) is, like a length squared, never negative.

On the axis is the factor \(\alpha\), on the vertical one the value of the form. The requirement of linearity is the line \(\alpha\,\tilde\ell(w)\) through zero. At \(\alpha = 1\) the curves meet at \(2003\) N m\(^2\). At \(\alpha = 2\) the requirement is \(4007\) N m\(^2\), in fact \(\tilde\ell(2w)\) lies on the parabola at \(8013\) N m\(^2\).

Linearity has a condition too. On the hanging bar, \(q = 6{,}010\) N/m and \(L = 10\) m, take \(\tilde\ell(w) = \int_0^L q\,w^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), which differs from \(\ell\) only in that \(w\) is squared. For \(w = x\) (\(x\) in metres) we have \(\tilde\ell(w) = q\,L^3/3 = 2003\) N m\(^2\). The requirement of the definition with \(\alpha = 2\) and \(\beta = 0\) would give \(\tilde\ell(2w) = 2\,\tilde\ell(w) = 4007\) N m\(^2\). In fact \(\tilde\ell(2w) = \int_0^L q\,(2w)^2\,\mathrm{d}x = 4 \cdot 2003 = 8013\) N m\(^2\), because the factor \(2\) is multiplied by itself in the square. The requirement therefore fails, \(\tilde\ell\) is not linear. For \(\ell(w) = \int_0^L q\,w\,\mathrm{d}x\) the function \(w\) stands to the first power and the factor \(2\) comes out in front of the integral.

The weak form of all three is thus one sentence. Let us write it for every task with such forms, since further on we shall also use it for the bar fixed at both ends, for beams and for the body.

All the fields among which we search form the space \(X\), drawn as a plane. The fields that satisfy the essential conditions lie on the shifted plane, since an essential condition prescribes a value and the zero field is not admissible. On it lies the solution \(u\). Test functions are zero wherever something is prescribed, so they form the space \(W\) through zero, and a shift by \(w\) stays on the admissible plane.

Definition 6.6 Weak form with a bilinear and a linear form (šibka oblika z bilinearno in linearno formo)

Let \(X\) be the vector space of fields among which the task seeks the solution, \(B\) a bilinear form and \(\ell\) a linear form on \(X\). For the bar \(X\) is the space of the continuous functions of definition 6.2 without the condition at the support, for the beam the space of functions with continuous \(w\), \(w'\) and \(w''\), for the body the space of continuously differentiable fields (definition 1.91). The essential conditions of the task prescribe the values of the field on the supported part of the boundary, for the beam possibly also of the slope. An admissible field (dopustno polje) is a field from \(X\) that satisfies the essential conditions. A test function is a field from \(X\) that is zero wherever the essential conditions prescribe something, for the beam together with the slope where this is prescribed. The sum and a multiple of test functions are again test functions, so they form a vector space \(W\). The weak form (šibka oblika) of the task is the task: find an admissible field \(u\) for which

\[B(u, w) = \ell(w) \qquad \text{for every } w \in W . \tag{6.4}\]

For the bar fixed at \(x = 0\) this is definition 6.2, for the beam equation (6.3) and for the body equation (4.52).

Source: EP (6.3.43) (p. 327), where the test function is the first argument of the form \(B\), which for a symmetric form is the same.

At the top is the deformed bar: \(w'\) is not zero everywhere, the area under \(EA\,w'^2\) is positive and so is \(B(w, w)\). For a rigid shift \(w' = 0\) and the area and the energy are zero. The fixed end prevents such a shift, since \(w(0) = 0\). For the beam the energy is zero for the line \(w = \alpha + \beta x\), for the body for a rigid motion, and the supports remove both.

We shall need one more property all the time: that \(B(w, w)\) is not negative and is zero only for \(w = 0\). Why? \(B(w, w)\) is twice the strain energy of the field \(w\) (bar and beam: because the energy is \(\tfrac12\,EA\,w'^2\) or \(\tfrac12\,EI\,w''^2\) per unit length, body: equation (3.70)). The energy is positive if the bar really deforms. Zero energy, however, means that the bar or the body deforms nowhere, so it only moves as a rigid body, and the supports do not allow this.

Lemma 6.7 Positivity of the energy (pozitivnost energije)

Let \(B\) be the bilinear form of one of the three tasks in the table and \(W\) the space of its test functions (definition 6.6), and let \(B(w, w) = 2U(w)\) be twice the strain energy of the field \(w\). Then \(B(w, w) \ge 0\) for every \(w \in W\), and \(B(w, w) = 0\) only for \(w = 0\), if the assumptions of the task hold:

  1. bar: \(EA > 0\) continuous on pieces, the bar fixed at least at one end,
  2. beam: \(EI > 0\) continuous, \(w\) and \(w'\) continuous, \(w''\) continuous, and the only straight line \(w = \alpha + \beta x\) in \(W\) is \(w = 0\) (for example for the clamp \(w(0) = w'(0) = 0\) or for the supports \(w(0) = w(L) = 0\)),
  3. body of isotropic material with \(E > 0\) and \(-1 < \nu < \tfrac12\), a connected interior of the body, and the only rigid motion \(\vek w = \vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\) (constant vector \(\vek a\), antisymmetric matrix \(\mat W\)) that is zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is \(\vek w = \vek 0\).
Proof

We must show non-negativity, and then in each case that zero energy implies the zero field.

In the panel for the bar the graph of \(EA\,w'^2\) lies on every piece above the axis, so every integral over a piece is non-negative. If at the point \(x_0\) the value is positive, then on a neighbourhood it is at least half of it and the rectangle under the curve has positive area. If the sum is zero, then \(w' = 0\) everywhere. In the panel for the beam \(w'' = 0\), so \(w'\) is constant and \(w\) is a line. In the panel for the body we take a point \(P\) and around it a small box on which \(\Phi_{\mathrm{w}} \ge \Phi_{\mathrm{w}}(P)/2\). If it is zero everywhere, the field is a rigid motion, which the face \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) stops.

  1. Bar. The integrand \(EA\,w'^2\) is not negative, so the integral over every piece is not negative either (lemma 3.54, item 4). Let the sum of the integrals over the pieces be zero. Since none is negative, each is zero. Take a piece between \(x_{\mathrm{k}-1}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\) on the horizontal axis \(x\). Suppose that \(w'(x_0) \ne 0\) at some point of a piece. Then the function \(EA\,w'^2\) is continuous on the piece and positive at \(x_0\), with the value \(p\). By continuity it is greater than \(p/2\) on a band around \(x_0\), so the integral over the piece is not smaller than the area \(p\,\delta\) of the rectangle under the graph and is positive, as in steps 6 and 7 of the proof of corollary 4.93. This is a contradiction. Therefore \(w' = 0\) on every piece, by corollary 1.86 \(w\) is constant on every piece, and since it is continuous, it is constant on the whole \([0, L]\). A test function is zero at the fixed end, so \(w = 0\).
  2. Beam. The same argument with \(EI\,w''^2\) gives \(w'' = 0\) on \([0, L]\). By corollary 1.86 \(w'\) is constant, \(w' = \beta\), and \(w - \beta x\) has derivative zero, so \(w = \alpha + \beta x\). This line is in \(W\), so by assumption \(w = 0\).
  3. Body. By theorem 3.64, item 1, the strain energy density is positive for every strain that is not zero, and by theorem 3.62, item 2, \(B(w, w) = 2\int_{\mathrm{V}} \Phi_{\mathrm{w}}\,\mathrm{d}V\), where \(\Phi_{\mathrm{w}}\) is the strain energy density (definition 3.59) for the strain of the field \(\vek w\), so \(B(w, w) \ge 0\). Let \(B(w, w) = 0\). The density \(\Phi_{\mathrm{w}}\) is continuous and non-negative, so it is zero at every point of the interior: if it were positive at a point \(P\), then by continuity it would be at least \(\Phi_{\mathrm{w}}(P)/2\) on a small box around \(P\), the integral over the box would be positive and by monotonicity (lemma 4.32, item 2) at most \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} \Phi_{\mathrm{w}}\,\mathrm{d}V = 0\), a contradiction, so the strain is zero at every point. By theorem 1.140 we have \(\vek w = \vek a + \mat W\,\vek r\) on the interior, and by continuity on the whole body. The field is zero on \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), so by assumption \(\vek w = \vek 0\).

Source: EP §6.2.5 (pp. 283, 287). The proof is not from a source, the bar we treated in steps 6 to 8 of the proof of corollary 4.93.

The cube with edge \(h\) is glued with its bottom face \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) to the table. On it we choose three points that do not lie on one line. If these points do not move, the cube cannot move as a rigid body. On the right is the hanging bar without \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\), for which a rigid shift is possible and the energy is zero.

The assumption about the supports is not empty. The cube of section 4.5.1 is glued with its bottom face to the table, and there \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) is the face \(z = 0\). If \(\vek a + \mat W\,\vek r = \vek 0\) at the points \((0, 0, 0)\), \((h, 0, 0)\) and \((0, h, 0)\), then \(\vek a = \vek 0\), \(\mat W\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek 0\) and \(\mat W\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = \vek 0\). An antisymmetric matrix with zero first two columns has, because of antisymmetry, zero first two rows as well, and its element \(W_{\mathrm{zz}}\) is zero, because the diagonal of an antisymmetric matrix is zero. So \(\mat W = \mat 0\) and the cube is held. The hanging bar as a body in section 4.5.1, however, has \(S_{\mathrm{u}}\) empty, and the energy is zero for a rigid motion. The bar in this section has a fixed end \(u(0) = 0\) and the lemma holds for it.

On the left the integration of a bar with constant stiffness and continuous load gives the solution in two steps from the load. On the right the horizontal axis is \(\|w\|^2\) and the vertical one is \(B(w, w)\). The elliptic form lies above the line \(\alpha\|w\|^2\), a merely positive form comes close to zero for some fields.

The existence of a solution of the weak form is for a bar and a beam with constant stiffness and continuous load guaranteed by integration, as we did it in chapters 4 and 5 (theorem 5.50). For a bar this holds also when the stiffness changes piece by piece: equilibrium gives \(N(x) = F + \int_{\mathrm{x}}^L q(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\), and the displacement is \(u(x) = \int_0^x N(t)/EA(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\), as for the bar with a step (section 6.1.4). For a beam with a variable stiffness and for a body the proof of existence is outside our computation. It needs the form \(B\) and the linear form \(\ell\) to be continuous and \(B\) to be elliptic, that is \(B(w, w) \ge \alpha\,\|w\|^2\) with the same number \(\alpha > 0\) for all \(w\) (with a norm that also measures the derivatives), which is more than the positivity of the lemma, and we leave it to chapter 11 (BATHE §4.3.4, PDF pp. 254-255, EP (6.2.41), p. 287, BATHE (4.78)). It also needs a complete space, the space of fields with square integrable derivatives (BATHE (4.72), EP p. 287). The solution lies in this larger space and can have an unbounded derivative with finite energy, like \(w = x^{3/4}\) on \([0, 1]\) with \(\int_0^1 w'^2\,\mathrm{d}x = 9/8\).

The solution lies in this larger space and can have an unbounded derivative with a finite energy. Such is \(w = x^{3/4}\) on \([0, 1]\): its derivative \(w' = \tfrac34\,x^{-1/4}\) grows beyond every bound as \(x\) goes to \(0\), but on the right axis \(w'^2\) the area under the graph is finite, \(\int_0^1 w'^2\,\mathrm{d}x = 9/8\). The narrow strip at \(x = 0\) up to \(x = 0{,}01\) contributes only \(0{,}1125\) to it, although the graph is highest there. The statements about the body in this chapter are therefore written with the words "if a solution exists".

On the axis is the shift \(\alpha\) in the direction \(w\), on the vertical one the change of energy. The quadratic term \(\tfrac12\,\alpha^2\,B(w, w)\) is a parabola opening upwards. If the weak form fails, the linear term tilts it and the lowest point lies at \(\alpha \ne 0\), where the energy is lower. If the weak form holds, the linear term is zero and the lowest point is at \(\alpha = 0\).

The weak form has a close connection with the total potential energy. The energy of the field \(u\) is \(\Pi(u) = \tfrac12\,B(u, u) - \ell(u)\), for the bar equation (4.63). Its difference between the fields \(u + \alpha w\) and \(u\) is \(\alpha\,\big(B(u, w) - \ell(w)\big) + \tfrac12\,\alpha^2\,B(w, w)\), which follows from bilinearity and symmetry. The term with \(\alpha\) is zero exactly when the weak form holds for \(w\). The weak form is therefore the condition that the energy changes, under a displacement in the direction of every test function, only by the term with \(\alpha^2\), and since the lemma on positivity says that this term is positive for \(\alpha \ne 0\) and \(w \ne 0\) when the supports meet its assumptions, and since the difference \(v - u\) of two admissible fields is a test function (we take \(w = v - u\) and \(\alpha = 1\)), the field is then the lowest among all admissible ones. We use this connection in the section where we find the free numbers from the smallest energy.
